splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (requiring only one criterion to disqualify).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply divided on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means 'and' or 'or,' directly affecting whether defendants with certain criminal histories can avoid mandatory minimum sentences. The split leads to dramatically different sentencing outcomes depending on which circuit a defendant is prosecuted in.

positions.label: Conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' as conjunctive.

positions.label: Disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity should trump deference to agency interpretations of ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions. The Third Circuit held that deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity prevails. The Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright overruling Chevron casts further doubt on the deference-first approach.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor or Chevron deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive deference.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference applies even in criminal or sentencing contexts, and that lenity does not override a deferential reading of ambiguous guidelines provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, aiding and abetting, attempt) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation of the guideline entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Guidelines commentary expanding 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy is entitled to deference, given that the guideline text itself does not mention inchoate offenses. Some circuits defer to the commentary; others hold it impermissibly expands the guideline's plain text.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses is a permissible interpretation of the ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight under Stinson and Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands the guideline
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond the text, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) when the state schedule of controlled substances is broader than the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance at issue to be federally controlled or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with state drug convictions involving substances not on the federal schedule.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — state schedules suffice
positions.summary: Holds that there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the career offender guideline; a state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense even if the substance is not federally scheduled.

positions.label: Must involve federally controlled substance
positions.summary: Holds that a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines must involve a substance controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, so state convictions for substances not on the federal schedule do not qualify.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release. Some circuits, following Sentencing Commission policy statements, allow it; others, like the Seventh and Eighth Circuits, hold that non-retroactive changes in law cannot contribute to such a finding.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly when combined with other factors, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's amended policy statement at U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must challenge conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the duration of custody exclusively through habeas corpus, or whether they may also bring claims under civil rights statutes like Bivens or the APA.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging BOP decisions that affect the fact or duration of confinement, or whether other causes of action (e.g., Bivens, § 1983 for state prisoners, or APA) are also available. The Supreme Court left this question open in Preiser v. Rodriguez and has not resolved it.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive remedy for duration-of-confinement challenges
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's claim effectively challenges the fact or duration of confinement, habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy, precluding civil rights or APA claims.

positions.label: Conditions challenges cognizable outside habeas
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions may proceed under civil rights statutes or other causes of action even when they arguably affect the duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly consider punishment as a purpose of revocation sentences imposed upon revocation of supervised release, or whether revocation sentences are limited to the purposes enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation, while other circuits hold that punishment is not a permissible purpose of revocation sentences. Dissenters in the Sixth Circuit have noted this places that circuit at the extreme of the split.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may impose revocation sentences that expressly account for punishment of the supervised release violation.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences serve only the limited purposes identified in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e) and § 3553(a), which do not include punishment for the underlying violation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held it belongs to the estate, while other circuits have concluded the opposite, creating a split that affects debtors' incentives to convert in good faith.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A) and § 541(a), post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor, not the estate, consistent with § 348(f)'s purpose of protecting good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the applicable time limit to appeal a denial of attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment is the civil deadline (30 days) or the criminal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, though arising in a criminal case, is a civil matter for purposes of the appellate filing deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but the split persists among the circuits.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion arises in a criminal case and therefore the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate multiemployer pension plan withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the plan year, or whether actuaries may select assumptions after the measurement date. The outcome affects billions of dollars in withdrawal liability obligations for thousands of employers.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be determined as of the end of the prior plan year and cannot be selected after the statutory measurement date.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may adopt or change actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, so long as the assumptions are reasonable.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: New York Times Co. v. Newspaper & Mail Deliverers' Union Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervisory period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing guidelines calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of absconders each year.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled while the supervisee is a fugitive, so the clock does not run during the period of absconding.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release during absconding, and courts lack authority to create such a doctrine to extend punishment beyond the judgment's terms.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are divided 6-to-3 on whether § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on claims previously presented in habeas applies to federal prisoners under § 2255 in addition to § 2255(h)'s own gatekeeping requirements. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter standard than Congress may have intended for successive collateral attacks.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim previously presented.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions; they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have pre-election standing to challenge voting rules. The case addresses whether candidates suffer a cognizable injury-in-fact from election administration procedures and whether such disputes must wait until after the election to be adjudicated.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury from state laws that allegedly dilute lawful votes by allowing late-arriving ballots, giving them Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing to challenge ballot-receipt deadlines pre-election because they cannot show a concrete, particularized injury traceable to the challenged law.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable as a collateral order because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Other circuits have not uniformly recognized such orders as immediately appealable, creating tension in the law.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order warranting immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine because delayed review risks irreversible disclosure.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are interlocutory and not within the narrow class of collateral orders immediately appealable under Cohen, because post-judgment review or other mechanisms can adequately address the harm.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
